findings.title: Multiple crypto providers no longer fail fast; selection between equal-order providers is classpath-dependent and only logged at DEBUG
findings.body: detectProvider() previously threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was found on the classpath, which was a deliberate fail-fast guard (e.g. against having both keycloak-crypto-default and keycloak-crypto-fips1402 present). Now it silently picks the provider with the highest order(). All three in-tree providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider) return order() == 200, so when more than one of them is present the winner is decided by ServiceLoader encounter order, i.e. by classpath/JAR ordering, which is not deterministic across deployments. Concretely: a FIPS deployment that accidentally also has keycloak-crypto-default on the classpath can silently initialize and register the plain (non-FIPS) BouncyCastle provider instead of BCFIPS, with no error; the 'Ignored crypto providers' message is emitted only at DEBUG level so operators will not notice the wrong provider being used. Either give the providers distinct orders, break ties deterministically, or at least log the ignored providers at WARN.

findings.title: order() added as an abstract method breaks the public CryptoProvider SPI
findings.body: The new int order() method was added to the public CryptoProvider interface without a default implementation. CryptoProvider is an SPI intended to be implemented outside the Keycloak tree (the same repo has three implementations and third-party/forks exist, e.g. in the keycloak-client repo that this PR's description says will be synced later). Any existing compiled implementation of CryptoProvider will still load via ServiceLoader but will throw AbstractMethodError as soon as CryptoIntegration.detectProvider() calls order() on it during sorted(...), breaking initialization of those deployments at runtime, and source-level implementors fail to compile. Declaring it as default int order() { return 0; } would preserve backward compatibility while still allowing the authz-client provider (order 100) to lose against the built-in providers (order 200).

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JVM default KeyStore provider (usually SUN), violating the interface contract
findings.body: The CryptoProvider contract documents getBouncyCastleProvider() as '@return BouncyCastle security provider' (non-FIPS or FIPS BC). AuthzClientCryptoProvider implements it as KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which returns the default JCA keystore provider - typically SUN - not BouncyCastle. Any code path that obtains the provider via CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getBouncyCastleProvider() and uses it as BC (requesting BC-only algorithms like AES/GCM with BC semantics, PKCS7 padding, BCFKS keystores, or registering the returned provider) will now get a provider that does not implement those algorithms and fail with NoSuchAlgorithmException at a distance from the real cause. If BC is genuinely never needed in this provider, throwing UnsupportedOperationException like the other unsupported methods, or returning null after documenting it, would fail fast instead of silently returning a wrong provider.

findings.title: Provider only implements ECDSA r/s conversion, but registers globally and is latched by AuthzClient.create() for the whole JVM
findings.body: AuthzClientCryptoProvider throws UnsupportedOperationException for getAlgorithmProvider(), getPemUtils(), getKeyFactory(), getSignature(), getX509CertFactory(), createECParams(), etc. However it is registered through META-INF/services and AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now calls CryptoIntegration.init(...), which sets the JVM-wide static provider. keycloak-core code that authz-client users commonly exercise routes through these methods: org.keycloak.common.util.PemUtils' PEM key/certificate decoding goes through CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getPemUtils(), and JWS signing helpers go through getAlgorithmProvider()/getSignature(). Concretely, an application that uses only the authz-client artifact (the exact scenario this PR targets - no BouncyCastle-based provider on the classpath, so the order-100 stub wins) and configures signed-JWT client credentials (jwt client authenticator) will hit UnsupportedOperationException when decoding the PEM private key, a feature the authz-client supports. There is no test or analysis in the PR demonstrating that the implemented surface (only ECDSA r/s conversion) covers what the authz-client actually invokes through CryptoIntegration; at minimum the JWT client-credentials flow should be tested end-to-end with this provider as the only one on the classpath.

findings.title: ECDSA test round-trip is too weak to catch truncation/padding bugs and misses leading-zero edge cases
findings.body: The test only checks that concat -> DER -> concat is self-consistent (rsConcat == rsConcat2). It never asserts that the re-encoded DER equals the original minimal-DER signature produced by JCA (Arrays.equals(sign, asn1Des)), so a bug that truncates or mis-pads r/s on the concat side could still pass, since the same buggy conversion is applied in both directions. Additionally, each test signs once with a freshly generated key, so the probability of exercising the tricky edge cases - r or s whose encoding has a leading zero byte or is shorter than the curve length, which is exactly what the hand-rolled ASN.1Encoder/ASN1Decoder code must handle via integerToBytes and the len+1 zero-padding - is roughly 1/256 per component per run and effectively never happens. The test should loop over many signatures (or use fixed vectors with known leading-zero r/s values) and also assert DER equality against the original signature bytes.

findings.title: No test for the new order-based provider selection logic
findings.body: The core behavior change of this PR - CryptoIntegration now tolerates multiple CryptoProviders on the classpath and selects the one with the highest order() instead of throwing IllegalStateException - has no test coverage anywhere in the changed files. A regression in the comparator (e.g. dropping .reversed() would silently pick the lowest-order provider, meaning AuthzClientCryptoProvider would win over DefaultCryptoProvider in the testsuite) or in the tie-breaking would go unnoticed. A unit test should assert that with two providers of different order the higher one is selected, and document/assert the intended behavior for equal orders, since all three built-in providers currently return 200.

findings.title: Dead code: two ASN1Encoder instances created and immediately discarded in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: Lines 114-115 ('ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger); ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);') create encoders, write the integers into them, and throw the results away - the actual encoding happens in the return statement below. These are leftover no-op statements from an earlier iteration of the method; they allocate objects for nothing and suggest an incomplete edit. They should be removed so the method is not misleading.
